title: Money
subtitle: currency, cashpoint, owe, afford, save up, deposit
summary: Talk about money: notes and coins, your bank account, loans and what you can afford.

lesson.heading: Currency
lesson.text: The **currency** is the type of money used in a country. In the UK the currency is **sterling** (pounds); in America it is the **dollar**; in much of Europe it's the **euro**.

examples.text: Sterling is the **currency** of the UK.
How many euros do you get for a hundred **dollars**?

lesson.heading: Notes and coins
rows: fifty pence, usually spoken as fifty p
lesson.note: When the number and the money word come before a noun, we use no -s: a ten-pound note, not ~~a ten-pounds note~~.

lesson.heading: Managing your money
lesson.text: You keep your money in a **bank account**. If your account is **in credit**, you have money in it. A **cashpoint** is a machine where you can get money, and **cash** is money in the form of notes and coins. To **check** your account means to look at the details of it.

examples.text: I've had a **bank account** for a few years now, and I make sure my account is always **in credit**.
I go to the **cashpoint** once a week, so I always have some **cash** with me.
I **check** my account online once a week to see how much money I've got.

lesson.heading: Money problems
lesson.text: A **loan** is money you borrow, and you have to **pay** it **back**. **Fees** are money you pay to use something or for a service. If you **waste** money you use it badly, and if you **owe** money you have to pay it back.

examples.text: When I went to university, I had to get a student **loan** to pay my **fees**.
I had to make sure I didn't **waste** money, but by the time I finished my degree I **owed** a lot.
I don't have to **pay** it **back** until I get a job and I'm **earning** a reasonable **amount** of money.
examples.note: earn = receive money for the work you do; an amount = how much

lesson.heading: Saving and affording
lesson.text: If you **save up** for something, you keep money to buy it in the future. If you **can't afford** something, you don't have enough money to buy it.

examples.text: At the moment I'm **saving up** for a new laptop.
I'd love to have a car as well, but I **can't afford** it.
I've been putting money into my bank **account** every month.

lesson.heading: Accommodation
lesson.text: **Accommodation** means the places where you live or stay. A **deposit** is money you pay for something you are going to use, and you get it back at the end. Something that is **good value for money** is good for the amount you pay, and if someone **charges** you, they ask you to pay an amount of money.

examples.text: This year I'm **renting** a flat with three friends of mine.
We had to pay one month's **rent** as a **deposit**.
It's a nice place, quite **good value for money**.
The **landlord** isn't **charging** us to use his garage.

lesson.heading: rent and hire

left.label: rent
left.text: You pay to use something for a long period of time. The noun **rent** is the amount you pay.
examples: We **rent** a flat near the station.

right.label: hire
right.text: You pay to use something for a short period of time.
examples: I **hired** a bike for the day.
We **hired** a car when we were on holiday.

lesson.note: Both verbs are used with cars: we rented / hired a car on holiday.

lesson.text: Owe and own look similar but are very different: if you owe money, you have to pay it back; if you own something, it belongs to you.

exercises.prompt: Match each definition with the right word.

pairs.left: A flat, usually round piece of metal used as money
Money you borrow from a bank
Money you pay for a professional service
Money in the form of notes or coins
A machine where you can get money
The type of money used in a country

exercises.statement: If you are in credit, you have money in your bank account.
exercises.explanation: Correct. In credit = having money in the account.

exercises.statement: A five-pound note is worth less than a fifty-pence piece.
exercises.explanation: A five-pound note is worth much more: five pounds is 500 pence.

exercises.statement: If you waste money, you use it well.
exercises.explanation: If you waste money, you use it badly.

exercises.prompt: He's ___ 300 pounds a week in his job.
exercises.explanation: Earn = receive money for the work you do.

exercises.prompt: She ___ the money: she bought things she never used.
I'd like to come with you, but I can't ___ to go.
exercises.explanation: Can't afford something = not have enough money for it.

exercises.prompt: We looked at the bill and saw that he had ___ us 25 pounds.
exercises.explanation: Charge someone = ask them to pay an amount of money.

exercises.prompt: I've got to pay back a lot of money: I ___ the bank 2,000 pounds.
exercises.explanation: Owe money = have to pay it back.

exercises.prompt: I'm nearly 20 now, and I've been ___ for a car for the last two years.
exercises.hint: (two words - keeping money for the future)
exercises.explanation: Save up for something = keep money to buy it in the future.

exercises.prompt: I try to put exactly the same ___ into my bank account every month.
exercises.explanation: An amount is how much money there is: a reasonable amount, a large amount.

exercises.prompt: We only need a car for one day. We could ___ one.
exercises.explanation: We hire something for a short period of time, and rent something for a long period.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to explain when you pay a student loan back.
exercises.answer: I don't have to pay it back until I get a job.
exercises.explanation: Pay back = give the money you owe to the bank or the person who lent it.
